column4: Wearing face masks will stop the spread of covid 19
column7: As of October 2020, scientific consensus held that face masks reduce but do not completely stop the transmission of COVID-19. Masks were understood as one layer of a multi-layered mitigation strategy (alongside distancing, hand hygiene, and ventilation) that lowers the probability of viral transmission by blocking respiratory droplets, but they do not provide complete protection, especially with inconsistent use, improper fit, or lower-quality materials. Breakthrough transmission among masked individuals was already documented, and studies showed reduction rates rather than full prevention. The claim's absolute phrasing that masks 'will stop' spread overstates the actual evidence, which supported mask-wearing as risk-reducing, not as a guaranteed stop to transmission.

column4: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020) does not make it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support.
column7: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act 2020 removed abortion from the Crimes Act and treated it primarily as a health and regulatory matter, focusing on procedural and conscientious objection provisions. The Act itself does not contain an explicit clause requiring medical practitioners to provide life-saving care to infants who survive an abortion procedure. This gap was raised during parliamentary debate, with some MPs and advocacy groups noting the absence of a specific born-alive protection clause in the bill. The government's position was that existing general laws (such as those governing homicide and medical duty of care) would apply once a child is born alive, but these are not part of the Abortion Legislation Act itself. Therefore, the claim accurately reflects that the Act does not explicitly mandate such care within its own text.
column9:
Are babies born alive after an abortion in NZ entitled to  medical support? Yes. Once alive and living outside the mother's womb, the neonate is a legal person and has the same rights as any other person, and there is a requirement to provide health care in the same way as for any other neonate.
Does NZ  Abortion Legislation Act (2020) makes it a legal requirement that babies born alive after an abortion are given medical support ? False , as per the New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act (2020),  proposed amendment was voted down by 80 to 37 votes, so will not be part of the Bill.  If it was passed, then The amendment would have required that if a baby was born alive following a failed abortion, a qualified health practitioner or any other health practitioner present at the time the child is born, would have a duty to provide the child with appropriate medical care and treatment.

column7: Prior to September 2020, no Supreme Court justice had ever been nominated and confirmed after voting in a presidential election had already begun. In historical instances where vacancies occurred in the autumn of an election year, such as in 1864, presidents delayed nominations until after the election concluded.
column9:
When was the claim made? 27/09/2020
Has voting begun for state elections in the US? Forty-five states and the District of Columbia offer early in-person voting (including states with all-mail elections). Delaware has enacted early voting but it will not be in place until 2022. Five states do not offer pre-Election Day in-person voting options: Connecticut, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, and South Carolina.
Have Supreme Court justice nominees ever been installed while a president is running for reelection? In presidential election years, five justices have been nominated and installed by presidents who were running for reelection.
Have there been presidential election years in the US where Supreme court judges were nominated and installed The first nomination during an election year in the twentieth century came on March 13, 1912, when  President William Taft (a Republican) nominated Mahlon Pitney to succeed John Marshall Harlan, who died on October 14, 1911.  The Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Pitney on March 18, 1912, by a vote of fifty to twenty-six.

President Woodrow Wilson (a Democrat) made two nominations during 1916.  On January 28, 1916, Wilson nominated Louis Brandeis to replace Joseph Rucker Lamar, who died on January 2, 1916; the Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Brandeis on June 1, 1916, by a vote of forty-seven to twenty-two.  Charles Evans Hughes resigned from the Court on June 10, 1916 to run (unsuccessfully) for president as a Republican.  On July 14, 1916, Wilson nominated John Clarke to replace him; Clarke was confirmed unanimously ten days later.

On February 15, 1932, President Herbert Hoover (a Republican) nominated Benjamin Cardozo to succeed Oliver Wendell Holmes, who retired on January 12, 1932.  A Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Cardozo by a unanimous voice vote on February 24, 1932.

On January 4, 1940, President Franklin Roosevelt (a Democrat) nominated Frank Murphy to replace Pierce Butler, who died on November 16, 1939; Murphy was confirmed by a heavily Democratic Senate on January 16, 1940, by a voice vote.

On November 30, 1987, President Ronald Reagan (a Republican) nominated Justice Anthony Kennedy to fill the vacancy created by the retirement of Lewis Powell.  A Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Kennedy (who followed Robert Bork and Douglas Ginsburg as nominees for that slot) on February 3, 1988, by a vote of ninety-seven to zero.

column7: Prior to September 2020, no Supreme Court justice had ever been nominated and confirmed after voting in a presidential election had already begun. Delaware has enacted early voting but it will not be in place until 2022. Five states do not offer pre-Election Day in-person voting options: Connecticut, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, and South Carolina.
Have Supreme Court justice nominees ever been installed while a president is running for reelection? In presidential election years, five justices have been nominated and installed by presidents who were running for reelection.
Have there been presidential election years in the US where Supreme court judges were nominated and installed The first nomination during an election year in the twentieth century came on March 13, 1912, when  President William Taft (a Republican) nominated Mahlon Pitney to succeed John Marshall Harlan, who died on October 14, 1911.  The Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Pitney on March 18, 1912, by a vote of fifty to twenty-six.

President Woodrow Wilson (a Democrat) made two nominations during 1916.  On January 28, 1916, Wilson nominated Louis Brandeis to replace Joseph Rucker Lamar, who died on January 2, 1916; the Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Brandeis on June 1, 1916, by a vote of forty-seven to twenty-two.  Charles Evans Hughes resigned from the Court on June 10, 1916 to run (unsuccessfully) for president as a Republican.  On July 14, 1916, Wilson nominated John Clarke to replace him; Clarke was confirmed unanimously ten days later.

On February 15, 1932, President Herbert Hoover (a Republican) nominated Benjamin Cardozo to succeed Oliver Wendell Holmes, who retired on January 12, 1932.  A Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Cardozo by a unanimous voice vote on February 24, 1932.

On January 4, 1940, President Franklin Roosevelt (a Democrat) nominated Frank Murphy to replace Pierce Butler, who died on November 16, 1939; Murphy was confirmed by a heavily Democratic Senate on January 16, 1940, by a voice vote.

On November 30, 1987, President Ronald Reagan (a Republican) nominated Justice Anthony Kennedy to fill the vacancy created by the retirement of Lewis Powell.  A Democratic-controlled Senate confirmed Kennedy (who followed Robert Bork and Douglas Ginsburg as nominees for that slot) on February 3, 1988, by a vote of ninety-seven to zero.

column7: New Zealand's Abortion Legislation Act 2020 does not include a specific provision requiring medical support for infants born alive following an abortion procedure. An amendment proposed during the legislative process to mandate medical care in such circumstances was voted down by Parliament.
